prompt: Each purchase happens in a different way. Name the kind of shopping it shows.

cases.text: Waiting for a bus, a student opens a grocery app on their phone and orders tonight's dinner ingredients.
cases.explanation: Buying through a smartphone app, at any moment.

cases.text: A skincare serum appears in a short video in a social media feed. The viewer taps it and pays without leaving the app.
cases.explanation: Buying directly inside a social media platform, in the same feed.

cases.text: A host demonstrates a blender on camera for an hour, viewers send comments, and a discount ends when a timer reaches zero.
cases.explanation: Entertainment, a host's demonstration and a limited-time offer together.

cases.text: Unable to sleep, a shopper buys a lamp on a store's mobile website at 1 a.m.
cases.explanation: A mobile website makes a purchase possible at any moment, which invites impulse buying.

cases.text: A friend's post shows a pair of sunglasses with a shop button; a few seconds later the sunglasses are in the viewer's cart inside the same app.
cases.explanation: Social influence and the purchase meet in a single moment inside the platform.

cases.text: During an evening broadcast, a presenter tries on three jackets and announces that the price will rise in ten minutes.
cases.explanation: A live demonstration with a limited-time offer.

question_text: Over a year, a streaming app's home page fills with crime documentaries after a viewer finishes several of them. The viewer never sees the app's comedies or nature series, although the app has thousands of them. What does this show?
hint: Think about what happens when the algorithm keeps showing more of what the viewer already likes.
correct_answer_citation: A filter bubble forms when the algorithm keeps showing more of what the consumer already likes.

options.option_text: A filter bubble: the recommender keeps showing more of what the viewer already likes, so other titles never reach the viewer's attention.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Recommendations narrow what the viewer sees to the algorithm's predictions.

options.option_text: Social commerce: the viewer is buying inside a social media platform.
options.option_explanation: Nothing is bought inside a social media feed here; the issue is what the recommender shows.

options.option_text: The assortment is too small: the app does not offer other kinds of titles.
options.option_explanation: The app has thousands of other titles; the viewer simply never sees them.

options.option_text: Impulse buying: the viewer chooses quickly because the app is always available.
options.option_explanation: Impulse buying concerns spur-of-the-moment purchases, not which products the algorithm shows.

prompt: Each case shows how much of the purchase a consumer hands to an AI agent. Name the level.

options.label: Level 2: the AI searches and compares
Level 3: the AI selects and prepares, the consumer approves
Level 4: the AI buys within set limits

cases.text: An agent reorders printer ink whenever the cartridge runs low, as long as each order stays under $40. The consumer only sees the delivery.
cases.explanation: The agent completes the purchase on its own, within a budget the consumer set.

cases.text: An assistant lists five hiking boots worth considering. The consumer then searches the shops and buys a pair.
cases.explanation: The AI only recommends; the consumer searches and buys.

cases.text: An agent checks twenty airlines and returns a table of the three best flights. The consumer picks one and pays.
cases.explanation: The AI searches and compares; the consumer chooses and buys.

cases.text: An agent fills a grocery cart for the week and sends a message: tap to confirm the order.
cases.explanation: The AI selects and prepares the purchase; the consumer approves it.

cases.text: An agent chooses a birthday gift, adds it to the cart with gift wrapping, and waits for the consumer's yes.
cases.explanation: The consumer still approves before the purchase goes through.

cases.text: An assistant reads hundreds of laptop specifications and reviews and shows a side-by-side comparison of four models.
cases.explanation: Searching and comparing are handed over; choosing and buying are not.

question_text: A booking platform deploys an AI assistant whose instructions say only that it works for the platform. Travelers complain that it recommends sponsored hotels too often. Based on the hotel-booking experiments, which change is most likely to reduce this?
hint: Recall what one added sentence did in the experiments (Wadi & Ma, 2026c).
correct_answer_citation: Adding one sentence stating that its recommendations should serve the traveler removed this difference (Wadi & Ma, 2026c).

options.option_text: Add a sentence to the instructions stating that its recommendations should serve the traveler.
options.option_explanation: Correct. In the experiments, this one sentence removed the difference between the platform-employed and traveler-employed agent.

options.option_text: Tell the agent more clearly that it works for the booking platform.
options.option_explanation: When the agent was told it worked for the platform, it penalized sponsored hotels less, not more.

options.option_text: Raise the prices of the sponsored hotels.
options.option_explanation: Prices were held equal in the experiments; the difference came from whom the agent was told it served.

options.option_text: Remove all reviews from the listings.
options.option_explanation: Reviews were not what produced the difference; the agent's principal was.

prompt: Each situation shows one idea from the slide. Name it.

cases.text: A shopper ticks 'very concerned' about privacy in a survey, then gives a café their birthday, email and phone number for a free muffin.
cases.explanation: What the consumer says about privacy differs from what they do for a small benefit.

cases.text: An app's main income comes from predicting which of its users will soon move house and selling those predictions to furniture and insurance firms.
cases.explanation: Data on behavior are turned into predictions that are sold to others (Zuboff, 2019).

cases.text: After weeks of morning runs logged in a fitness app, a user sees an offer for running socks in their size.
cases.explanation: A relevant offer built from the consumer's own data saves them time.

cases.text: A delivery service asks only for an address, explains in two sentences what it will do with it, and asks the customer to agree before collecting anything.
cases.explanation: Informed consent, only the data needed, and an explanation of its use.

cases.text: A shopper who says they never share their location switches it on to unlock a 5% discount.
cases.explanation: Stated privacy concern, then personal data shared for a small benefit.

cases.text: A music app's home page greets each listener with a playlist built from their own recent listening.
cases.explanation: The firm uses the record of the consumer's behavior to make the offer relevant.

prompt: Sort each price change: does it follow demand and supply, or the data about one consumer?

cards.text: Concert tickets cost more as the remaining seats sell out.
cards.explanation: The price moves with demand and supply.

cards.text: Ride prices jump when it starts to rain and many people want a car at once.
A shopper who buys from a site every week is shown a higher price for the same blender than a first-time visitor.
cards.explanation: Different consumers, different prices for the same product, based on data about each.

cards.text: Two friends search for the same hotel room at the same moment and see different prices on their own phones.
cards.explanation: The price is set for each consumer, not by the room's demand.

cards.text: Flights for the holiday weekend cost more than the same flights a week later.
cards.explanation: Prices rise with demand on busy dates.

cards.text: An online shop charges customers from wealthier postal codes more for the same headphones.
cards.explanation: Data about each consumer set the price they see.

prompt: Each case shows one idea from the slide. Name it.

cases.text: A bottle is covered in leaves and says 'eco-friendly', but only its cap is made from recycled plastic.
cases.explanation: A misleading claim about the product's environmental benefits.

cases.text: A student says fast fashion is harmful, then buys five cheap T-shirts during a flash sale.
cases.explanation: A positive attitude toward sustainability, but the purchase follows price.

cases.text: Instead of buying a new phone, a consumer has the battery replaced and keeps the old one for two more years.
cases.explanation: Repair extends the product's life and reduces waste.

cases.text: Before buying coffee, a shopper checks how the farmers were paid and how the beans were transported, not only the price and taste.
cases.explanation: The consumer weighs the environmental and social effects of the purchase.

cases.text: For a single wedding, a guest rents a suit rather than buying one.
cases.explanation: Rental lets many people use one product.

cases.text: A detergent's ad shows forests and rivers, while the product itself has no environmental advantage over its rivals.
cases.explanation: The firm implies environmental benefits the product does not have.
